CHILD CUSTODY JURISDICTION (UCCJEA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION OF JURISDICTIONAL FACTS UNDER THE UCCJEA
I, Jordan Lee, am a party to a pending or about-to-be-filed child custody proceeding in San Francisco County County, California, concerning Casey Lee. To the best of my knowledge and belief, the following are Casey Lee's places of residence during the last five years, including the person(s) Casey Lee lived with and the approximate dates: Lived in Nevada from 2020-2023, California since 2023. Casey Lee currently resides in California. The other parent (or other person claiming custody or visitation rights) is Taylor Morgan. To the best of my knowledge and belief, the following custody or visitation proceeding(s) concerning Casey Lee, if any, are now pending or have previously been filed in this or another state, including the court, case number, and nature of the proceeding: None known. To the best of my knowledge and belief, the following person(s), other than a party to this proceeding, currently have physical custody of Casey Lee or claim custody or visitation rights, if any: None known. This declaration collects the same category of jurisdictional facts California's own Judicial Council UCCJEA declaration form (form FL-105) asks for, for use alongside an actual filing in the appropriate California superior court; it does not itself establish that any particular state is Casey Lee's home state or that a California court has jurisdiction over this matter -- only a court, applying Family Code section 3421 (and, where applicable, section 3424) to these facts, can make that determination.

HOME STATE JURISDICTION: THE PRIMARY BASIS FOR AN INITIAL CUSTODY DETERMINATION
California's Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (UCCJEA), Family Code sections 3400-3465, defines “home state” as the state in which a child lived with a parent or a person acting as a parent for at least six consecutive months immediately before the commencement of a child custody proceeding; for a child under six months old, the term instead means the state in which the child has lived from birth with any of those persons; and a period of temporary absence by the child or a listed adult counts as part of that period rather than interrupting it. Home-state status is the primary jurisdictional basis for an initial child custody determination: except when temporary emergency jurisdiction applies (addressed separately in this document), a California court has jurisdiction to make an initial custody determination if California is the child's home state on the date the proceeding commences, or was the child's home state within the six months before commencement and the child is now absent from California but a parent or a person acting as a parent continues to live here. The UCCJEA lists this home-state basis first among the statutory grounds for initial jurisdiction; the alternative bases available when no state qualifies as the home state are addressed in a separate clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Home state” means the state in which a child lived with a parent or a person acting as a parent for at least six consecutive months immediately before the commencement of a child custody proceeding. In the case of a child less than six months of age, the term means the state in which the child lived from birth with any of the persons mentioned. A period of temporary absence of any of the mentioned persons is part of the period."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3402(g), the statutory definition of "home state" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3402.)
  "This state is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding, or was the home state of the child within six months before the commencement of the proceeding and the child is absent from this state but a parent or person acting as a parent continues to live in this state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3421(a)(1), home state as the primary basis for jurisdiction to make an initial custody determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3421.)

UNIFORM CHILD CUSTODY JURISDICTION AND ENFORCEMENT ACT [3400 - 3465]"), so the section range given in this document's framing is correct as stated, not merely assumed. This clause cites two separately numbered statutory sections -- Family Code section 3402(g) (definitions, Chapter 1) and section 3421(a)(1) (initial jurisdiction, Chapter 2) -- both within the same 1999 enactment (Stats. 1999, Ch. 867) that created this part, so they are independent in the sense of being separately numbered provisions but not in the sense of separately-enacted law. Both sections were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and each quote was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of the fetched section text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act actually defines and applies the home-state concept -- not a claim about which state's courts have jurisdiction over any specific child or family, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment uses identical section numbers or wording (nearly all U.S. states have enacted some version of the UCCJEA, but California's specific codification, cited here, is what this document describes). This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which state is a specific child's home state or that a California court has jurisdiction over any specific custody matter -- only a court, applying section 3421 to the facts of a filed case, can make that determination. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear statutory definitions rather than by contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

ALTERNATIVE JURISDICTIONAL BASES WHEN NO STATE QUALIFIES AS THE HOME STATE
When no state -- including California -- qualifies as the child's home state under the definition addressed in a separate clause, or the home-state court has declined jurisdiction in favor of a more appropriate forum, Family Code section 3421(a)(2) permits a California court to make an initial custody determination on a "significant connection" basis, but only if two conditions are both true: the child and the child's parents (or the child and at least one parent or person acting as a parent) have a significant connection with California other than mere physical presence, and substantial evidence is available in California concerning the child's care, protection, training, and personal relationships. If every court with jurisdiction under the home-state or significant-connection bases has declined to exercise it on the ground that California is the more appropriate forum, section 3421(a)(3) supplies a further basis (not separately quoted here). And if no other state would have jurisdiction under any of the first three bases, section 3421(a)(4) makes California's jurisdiction available by elimination. Section 3421(b) then states that this list -- home state, significant connection, forum-declination, and no-other-state-has-jurisdiction -- is the exclusive jurisdictional basis for an initial custody determination by a California court: physical presence of the child in California, or personal jurisdiction over a parent, is by itself neither necessary nor sufficient.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A court of another state does not have jurisdiction under paragraph (1), or a court of the home state of the child has declined to exercise jurisdiction on the grounds that this state is the more appropriate forum under Section 3427 or 3428, and both of the following are true: (A) The child and the child’s parents, or the child and at least one parent or a person acting as a parent, have a significant connection with this state other than mere physical presence. (B) Substantial evidence is available in this state concerning the child’s care, protection, training, and personal relationships."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3421(a)(2), the significant-connection basis for initial jurisdiction when no state is the home state (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3421.)
  "No court of any other state would have jurisdiction under the criteria specified in paragraph (1), (2), or (3). (b) Subdivision (a) is the exclusive jurisdictional basis for making a child custody determination by a court of this state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3421(a)(4)-(b), the default basis when no other state would have jurisdiction, and the exclusivity of this list of bases (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3421.)

Correction/verification of the user's framing: the "significant connection" test does have two conjunctive prongs, as the user's framing anticipated, but this clause states them as actually written in the statute (a significant connection with the state other than mere physical presence, plus the availability of substantial evidence in the state concerning the child's care, protection, training, and personal relationships) rather than assuming their content in advance; California's UCCJEA also states a third and fourth basis (forum-declination and no-other-state-would-have-jurisdiction) not always emphasized in general summaries of the "significant connection" test, and this clause includes them. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the UCCJEA structures its jurisdictional list -- not a claim about which state's courts have jurisdiction over any specific child, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment states these bases in identical language. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any of these bases is satisfied for a specific child or family -- only a court can make that determination on the facts before it. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear statutory text, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

EXCLUSIVE, CONTINUING JURISDICTION TO MODIFY A CUSTODY DETERMINATION
Once a California court has made a child custody determination consistent with the initial-jurisdiction rules addressed elsewhere in this document, Family Code section 3422(a) gives that court "exclusive, continuing jurisdiction" over the determination -- meaning California, and no other state, generally retains the power to modify it -- until one of two things happens: a California court itself determines that neither the child, nor the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent, any longer has a significant connection with California and that substantial evidence concerning the child's care, protection, training, and personal relationships is no longer available here; or a California court or a court of another state determines that the child, the child's parents, and any person acting as a parent no longer presently reside in California. This is structurally similar to, but a genuinely separate statute from, UIFSA's continuing-exclusive-jurisdiction concept for child and spousal support (addressed in this corpus's separate UIFSA Registration Information Sheet document): the UCCJEA's version turns on significant connection and evidence availability, or on where the child, the parents, and any person acting as a parent currently reside, not on where an individual "obligor" or "obligee" resides, and it has no party-consent mechanism paralleling UIFSA's. Correspondingly, Family Code section 3423 states that another state's court generally may not modify a California custody determination unless that other state would itself have jurisdiction to make an initial determination and either California determines it no longer has exclusive, continuing jurisdiction (or that the other state is a more convenient forum), or a court determines that the child, the child's parents, and any person acting as a parent no longer reside in California.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided in Section 3424, a court of this state that has made a child custody determination consistent with Section 3421 or 3423 has exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over the determination until either of the following occurs: (1) A court of this state determines that neither the child, nor the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent have a significant connection with this state and that substantial evidence is no longer available in this state concerning the child’s care, protection, training, and personal relationships. (2) A court of this state or a court of another state determines that the child, the child’s parents, and any person acting as a parent do not presently reside in this state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3422(a), the conditions under which California retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction to modify a custody determination it made (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3422.)
  "Except as otherwise provided in Section 3424, a court of this state may not modify a child custody determination made by a court of another state unless a court of this state has jurisdiction to make an initial determination under paragraph (1) or (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3421 and either of the following determinations is made: (a) The court of the other state determines it no longer has exclusive, continuing jurisdiction under Section 3422 or that a court of this state would be a more convenient forum under Section 3427. (b) A court of this state or a court of the other state determines that the child, the child’s parents, and any person acting as a parent do not presently reside in the other state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3423, when another state's court may modify a California custody determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3423.)

This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether a specific California custody determination retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction, or whether another state may modify it -- only a court can make that determination on the facts before it. TEMPORARY EMERGENCY JURISDICTION: A SEPARATE, TIME-LIMITED BASIS DISTINCT FROM THE EX PARTE ORDER PROCEDURE
The UCCJEA contains its own, separate jurisdictional basis -- distinct from home-state, significant-connection, and exclusive-continuing jurisdiction, all addressed elsewhere in this document -- for a California court to act even when it otherwise lacks jurisdiction under those rules. Family Code section 3424(a) gives a California court "temporary emergency jurisdiction" if the child is physically present in California and either the child has been abandoned, or it is necessary in an emergency to protect the child because the child (or a sibling or parent of the child) is subjected to, or threatened with, mistreatment or abuse, or because the child has been unable to obtain gender-affirming health care or gender-affirming mental health care as statutorily defined. This jurisdictional basis is genuinely distinct from this corpus's separate Emergency (Ex Parte) Custody Order Information Sheet document, which addresses the procedural mechanism -- California Rules of Court, rule 5.151, and Family Code section 3064's immediate-harm standard -- for requesting an emergency order without advance notice to the other parent in a case where a California court already has jurisdiction; section 3424 instead addresses whether a California court has jurisdiction to act on an emergency basis at all, including in a case where no other jurisdictional basis under this document is available. An order made under section 3424 is expressly temporary: if no other state's court with jurisdiction under the ordinary rules has yet acted, section 3424(b) states that the California emergency order remains in effect only until an order is obtained from a court of a state having jurisdiction under those ordinary rules, unless no such proceeding is commenced and California itself becomes the child's home state, in which case the order can become a final determination. Section 3424(d), not quoted here, additionally requires a California court exercising this emergency jurisdiction to immediately communicate with the court of any state that already has, or is exercising, jurisdiction under the ordinary rules.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A court of this state has temporary emergency jurisdiction if the child is present in this state and the child has been abandoned or it is necessary in an emergency to protect the child because the child, or a sibling or parent of the child, is subjected to, or threatened with, mistreatment or abuse, or because the child has been unable to obtain gender-affirming health care or gender-affirming mental health care, as defined by Section 16010.2 of the Welfare and Institutions Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3424(a), the grounds for temporary emergency jurisdiction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3424.)
  "If there is no previous child custody determination that is entitled to be enforced under this part and a child custody proceeding has not been commenced in a court of a state having jurisdiction under Sections 3421 to 3423, inclusive, a child custody determination made under this section remains in effect until an order is obtained from a court of a state having jurisdiction under Sections 3421 to 3423, inclusive."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3424(b), the temporary, time-limited duration of an order made under emergency jurisdiction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3424.)

This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that a specific set of facts satisfies section 3424's emergency standard, or that a California court will exercise this jurisdiction -- only a court can make that determination.

REGISTERING AN OUT-OF-STATE CUSTODY DETERMINATION FOR ENFORCEMENT UNDER THE UCCJEA
Distinct from UIFSA's own registration mechanism for enforcing an out-of-state support order (addressed in this corpus's separate UIFSA Registration Information Sheet document), the UCCJEA has its own, separate registration mechanism -- a different statute -- for enforcing another state's custody determination in California. Family Code section 3445(a) allows a child custody determination issued by a court of another state to be registered in California, with or without a simultaneous request for enforcement, by sending to the appropriate California court: a letter or other document requesting registration; two copies (one certified) of the determination, together with a statement under penalty of perjury that, to the best of the requester's knowledge, the order has not been modified; and (except as otherwise provided elsewhere in the UCCJEA for certain safety-sensitive cases) the name and address of the person seeking registration and of any parent or person acting as a parent who was awarded custody or visitation in the determination. Once registered, section 3446 states the registered determination's effect: a California court may grant any relief normally available under California law to enforce it, and shall recognize and enforce -- but, except in accordance with the jurisdiction chapter addressed elsewhere in this document, may not modify -- a registered custody determination of another state's court. Registration also triggers a contest procedure: section 3445(c) requires the notice served on the other parties to state that a hearing to contest the registration's validity must be requested within 20 days of service, and that failing to timely contest results in the determination being confirmed by operation of law and precludes later contesting any matter that could have been raised at registration.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) A child custody determination issued by a court of another state may be registered in this state, with or without a simultaneous request for enforcement, by sending all of the following to the appropriate court in this state: (1) A letter or other document requesting registration. (2) Two copies, including one certified copy, of the determination sought to be registered, and a statement under penalty of perjury that to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person seeking registration the order has not been modified. (3) Except as otherwise provided in Section 3429, the name and address of the person seeking registration and any parent or person acting as a parent who has been awarded custody or visitation in the child custody determination sought to be registered."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3445(a), the records that must be sent to register another state's custody determination in California (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3445.)
  "(c) The notice required by paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) shall state all of the following: (1) That a registered determination is enforceable as of the date of the registration in the same manner as a determination issued by a court of this state. (2) That a hearing to contest the validity of the registered determination must be requested within 20 days after service of the notice. (3) That failure to contest the registration will result in confirmation of the child custody determination and preclude further contest of that determination with respect to any matter that could have been asserted."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3445(c), the required notice of the 20-day deadline to contest registration, and confirmation by operation of law if uncontested (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3445.)
  "(a) A court of this state may grant any relief normally available under the law of this state to enforce a registered child custody determination made by a court of another state. (b) A court of this state shall recognize and enforce, but may not modify, except in accordance with Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 3421), a registered child custody determination of a court of another state."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3446(a)-(b), the effect of a registered custody determination: enforceable, but not modifiable outside the jurisdiction rules (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3446.)

This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the UCCJEA structures registration and enforcement of another state's custody determination -- not a claim about which state's courts have jurisdiction over any specific determination, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment uses identical procedures or deadlines. This document is informational only: it does not itself register, enforce, confirm, or contest any custody determination. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear statutory text, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

SIMULTANEOUS PROCEEDINGS IN TWO STATES: DEFERENCE AND REQUIRED COMMUNICATION
The UCCJEA directly addresses what happens if custody proceedings concerning the same child are filed in two different states at roughly the same time. Family Code section 3426(a) states that, except when temporary emergency jurisdiction applies, a California court may not exercise jurisdiction over a custody proceeding if, at the time the California proceeding commences, a proceeding concerning the same child's custody has already been commenced in another state whose court has jurisdiction substantially in conformity with the UCCJEA -- unless that other proceeding has been terminated, or the other state's court has stayed its own proceeding because it has determined California is the more convenient forum. Section 3426(b), not separately quoted here, makes this a mandatory, not merely discretionary, screening step: before hearing a custody proceeding, a California court must examine the court documents and other information the parties have supplied and, if it determines a qualifying proceeding is already pending in another state, must stay its own proceeding and communicate with that state's court; if the other court does not determine that California is the more appropriate forum, the California court must dismiss its proceeding. This deference-and-communication structure depends on the general authority California courts have, under Family Code section 3410(a), to communicate directly with a court of another state concerning a proceeding arising under the UCCJEA -- a distinct, more general communication provision (in the UCCJEA's general-provisions chapter) than section 3426's specific simultaneous-proceedings rule.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided in Section 3424, a court of this state may not exercise its jurisdiction under this chapter if, at the time of the commencement of the proceeding, a proceeding concerning the custody of the child has been commenced in a court of another state having jurisdiction substantially in conformity with this part, unless the proceeding has been terminated or is stayed by the court of the other state because a court of this state is a more convenient forum under Section 3427."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3426(a), the bar on exercising jurisdiction while a conforming proceeding is already pending in another state (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3426.)
  "(a) A court of this state may communicate with a court in another state concerning a proceeding arising under this part."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 3410(a), the general authority for a California court to communicate with another state's court (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=3410.)

Both were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and each quote was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of the fetched section text. This clause quotes only section 3426(a) directly and describes, without a separate quoted citation, section 3426(b)'s mandatory stay-and-communicate procedure and section 3426(c)'s separate rule for simultaneous enforcement/modification proceedings (a related but distinct scenario from two competing proceedings both seeking an initial or modified determination, not covered by this clause's quoted text). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the UCCJEA structures deference between simultaneous proceedings -- not a claim about which state's courts should hear a specific two-state dispute, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment states this rule in identical language. If every court with jurisdiction under the home-state or significant-connection bases has declined to exercise it on the ground that California is the more appropriate forum, section 3421(a)(3) supplies a further basis (not separately quoted here). And if no other state would have jurisdiction under any of the first three bases, section 3421(a)(4) makes California's jurisdiction available by elimination. Section 3421(b) then states that this list -- home state, significant connection, forum-declination, and no-other-state-has-jurisdiction -- is the exclusive jurisdictional basis for an initial custody determination by a California court: physical presence of the child in California, or personal jurisdiction over a parent, is by itself neither necessary nor sufficient.

expectedJSON.body: Once a California court has made a child custody determination consistent with the initial-jurisdiction rules addressed elsewhere in this document, Family Code section 3422(a) gives that court "exclusive, continuing jurisdiction" over the determination -- meaning California, and no other state, generally retains the power to modify it -- until one of two things happens: a California court itself determines that neither the child, nor the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent, any longer has a significant connection with California and that substantial evidence concerning the child's care, protection, training, and personal relationships is no longer available here; or a California court or a court of another state determines that the child, the child's parents, and any person acting as a parent no longer presently reside in California. This is structurally similar to, but a genuinely separate statute from, UIFSA's continuing-exclusive-jurisdiction concept for child and spousal support (addressed in this corpus's separate UIFSA Registration Information Sheet document): the UCCJEA's version turns on significant connection and evidence availability, or on where the child, the parents, and any person acting as a parent currently reside, not on where an individual "obligor" or "obligee" resides, and it has no party-consent mechanism paralleling UIFSA's. Correspondingly, Family Code section 3423 states that another state's court generally may not modify a California custody determination unless that other state would itself have jurisdiction to make an initial determination and either California determines it no longer has exclusive, continuing jurisdiction (or that the other state is a more convenient forum), or a court determines that the child, the child's parents, and any person acting as a parent no longer reside in California.

(2) A court of this state or a court of another state determines that the child, the child’s parents, and any person acting as a parent do not presently reside in this state.

(b) A court of this state or a court of the other state determines that the child, the child’s parents, and any person acting as a parent do not presently reside in the other state.

expectedJSON.body: The UCCJEA contains its own, separate jurisdictional basis -- distinct from home-state, significant-connection, and exclusive-continuing jurisdiction, all addressed elsewhere in this document -- for a California court to act even when it otherwise lacks jurisdiction under those rules. Family Code section 3424(a) gives a California court "temporary emergency jurisdiction" if the child is physically present in California and either the child has been abandoned, or it is necessary in an emergency to protect the child because the child (or a sibling or parent of the child) is subjected to, or threatened with, mistreatment or abuse, or because the child has been unable to obtain gender-affirming health care or gender-affirming mental health care as statutorily defined. This jurisdictional basis is genuinely distinct from this corpus's separate Emergency (Ex Parte) Custody Order Information Sheet document, which addresses the procedural mechanism -- California Rules of Court, rule 5.151, and Family Code section 3064's immediate-harm standard -- for requesting an emergency order without advance notice to the other parent in a case where a California court already has jurisdiction; section 3424 instead addresses whether a California court has jurisdiction to act on an emergency basis at all, including in a case where no other jurisdictional basis under this document is available. An order made under section 3424 is expressly temporary: if no other state's court with jurisdiction under the ordinary rules has yet acted, section 3424(b) states that the California emergency order remains in effect only until an order is obtained from a court of a state having jurisdiction under those ordinary rules, unless no such proceeding is commenced and California itself becomes the child's home state, in which case the order can become a final determination. Section 3424(d), not quoted here, additionally requires a California court exercising this emergency jurisdiction to immediately communicate with the court of any state that already has, or is exercising, jurisdiction under the ordinary rules.

citations.quote: (a) A court of this state has temporary emergency jurisdiction if the child is present in this state and the child has been abandoned or it is necessary in an emergency to protect the child because the child, or a sibling or parent of the child, is subjected to, or threatened with, mistreatment or abuse, or because the child has been unable to obtain gender-affirming health care or gender-affirming mental health care, as defined by Section 16010.2 of the Welfare and Institutions Code.

citations.quote: If there is no previous child custody determination that is entitled to be enforced under this part and a child custody proceeding has not been commenced in a court of a state having jurisdiction under Sections 3421 to 3423, inclusive, a child custody determination made under this section remains in effect until an order is obtained from a court of a state having jurisdiction under Sections 3421 to 3423, inclusive.

expectedJSON.body: Distinct from UIFSA's own registration mechanism for enforcing an out-of-state support order (addressed in this corpus's separate UIFSA Registration Information Sheet document), the UCCJEA has its own, separate registration mechanism -- a different statute -- for enforcing another state's custody determination in California. Family Code section 3445(a) allows a child custody determination issued by a court of another state to be registered in California, with or without a simultaneous request for enforcement, by sending to the appropriate California court: a letter or other document requesting registration; two copies (one certified) of the determination, together with a statement under penalty of perjury that, to the best of the requester's knowledge, the order has not been modified; and (except as otherwise provided elsewhere in the UCCJEA for certain safety-sensitive cases) the name and address of the person seeking registration and of any parent or person acting as a parent who was awarded custody or visitation in the determination. Once registered, section 3446 states the registered determination's effect: a California court may grant any relief normally available under California law to enforce it, and shall recognize and enforce -- but, except in accordance with the jurisdiction chapter addressed elsewhere in this document, may not modify -- a registered custody determination of another state's court. Registration also triggers a contest procedure: section 3445(c) requires the notice served on the other parties to state that a hearing to contest the registration's validity must be requested within 20 days of service, and that failing to timely contest results in the determination being confirmed by operation of law and precludes later contesting any matter that could have been raised at registration.

citations.quote: (a) A child custody determination issued by a court of another state may be registered in this state, with or without a simultaneous request for enforcement, by sending all of the following to the appropriate court in this state: (1) A letter or other document requesting registration. (2) Two copies, including one certified copy, of the determination sought to be registered, and a statement under penalty of perjury that to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person seeking registration the order has not been modified. (3) Except as otherwise provided in Section 3429, the name and address of the person seeking registration and any parent or person acting as a parent who has been awarded custody or visitation in the child custody determination sought to be registered.

(2) That a hearing to contest the validity of the registered determination must be requested within 20 days after service of the notice. (3) That failure to contest the registration will result in confirmation of the child custody determination and preclude further contest of that determination with respect to any matter that could have been asserted.

(b) A court of this state shall recognize and enforce, but may not modify, except in accordance with Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 3421), a registered child custody determination of a court of another state.

expectedJSON.body: The UCCJEA directly addresses what happens if custody proceedings concerning the same child are filed in two different states at roughly the same time. Family Code section 3426(a) states that, except when temporary emergency jurisdiction applies, a California court may not exercise jurisdiction over a custody proceeding if, at the time the California proceeding commences, a proceeding concerning the same child's custody has already been commenced in another state whose court has jurisdiction substantially in conformity with the UCCJEA -- unless that other proceeding has been terminated, or the other state's court has stayed its own proceeding because it has determined California is the more convenient forum. Section 3426(b), not separately quoted here, makes this a mandatory, not merely discretionary, screening step: before hearing a custody proceeding, a California court must examine the court documents and other information the parties have supplied and, if it determines a qualifying proceeding is already pending in another state, must stay its own proceeding and communicate with that state's court; if the other court does not determine that California is the more appropriate forum, the California court must dismiss its proceeding. This deference-and-communication structure depends on the general authority California courts have, under Family Code section 3410(a), to communicate directly with a court of another state concerning a proceeding arising under the UCCJEA -- a distinct, more general communication provision (in the UCCJEA's general-provisions chapter) than section 3426's specific simultaneous-proceedings rule.
